summary: Specifies OCB, a shared-key block-cipher-based encryption scheme that provides confidentiality and authenticity for the data and authenticity for associated data. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

eli5.summary: This is a way to lock a message so no one can read it and no one can secretly change it, using one shared secret key in a single pass.

questions: what tag lengths does ocb support
subtitle: A block-cipher mode that encrypts and authenticates data in a single pass, with room to authenticate unencrypted headers too.

tldr.problem: Protecting data usually means combining separate encryption and authentication mechanisms, which is slower and easier to misuse. Network packets also carry unencrypted data, such as routing information, that still needs protecting.
tldr.mechanism: OCB is an authenticated-encryption-with-associated-data (AEAD) mode built on a 128-bit block cipher and a single key. It encrypts the plaintext and authenticates it together with the associated data and a nonce, appending an authentication tag.
tldr.outcome: OCB gives provable security if the block cipher is secure, but a nonce must never repeat under one key, and a key should encrypt at most 2^48 blocks.

today: RFC 7253 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed in its metadata. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group and defines OCB as it was published in May 2014.

sections.title: What OCB Provides
sections.content:
Authenticated encryption (AE) schemes give confidentiality and authentication together. Integrated schemes are less likely to be misused than separate encryption and authentication, and they can be significantly faster. When a scheme can also authenticate unencrypted associated data, such as a packet's routing information, it is an AEAD scheme.

OCB needs one key K and a block cipher with a 128-bit block size. The plaintext P and associated data A can have any bit length, and A may be empty. The ciphertext is a core of the same length as P plus an authentication tag, and this document writes it as the concatenation ciphertext-core || tag. On average OCB uses about a + m + 1.02 block-cipher calls, where a and m are the block lengths of A and P. It is online, parallelizable and provably secure assuming the block cipher is secure.

This version is called OCB3 in the 2011 paper and refines two earlier schemes from 2001 and 2004. The only difference from the paper is that the tag length is encoded into the internally formatted nonce. The CFRG judged it suitable for providing confidentiality and authentication.
sections.eli5: OCB seals a message and checks it hasn't been tampered with in one pass, like a lunchbox that is both locked and has a tamper-proof sticker.

sections.title: Parameters and Named Variants
sections.content:
Each OCB variant fixes two global parameters: a block cipher with 128-bit blocks (which defines KEYLEN, ENCIPHER and DECIPHER) and the tag length TAGLEN, which may be any value up to 128. A longer tag gives stronger assurance of authenticity, but each ciphertext is longer than its plaintext by exactly TAGLEN bits.

The RFC names nine AES-based sets: AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256, each with a 128, 96 or 64 bit tag, for example AEAD_AES_128_OCB_TAGLEN128. For the RFC 5116 interface, the maximum plaintext, associated data and ciphertext sizes are unbounded, the nonce is 1 to 15 bytes, and the key is 16, 24 or 32 bytes for AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256.
sections.eli5: You pick the size of the lock (the cipher) and the size of the seal (the tag). A bigger seal is harder to fake but makes the message a little longer.

sections.title: Encrypt, Decrypt and Hash
sections.content:
The RFC gives pseudocode for three functions. HASH processes the associated data into a 128-bit sum, and returns 128 zero bits when the data is empty. OCB-ENCRYPT takes the key K, a nonce N of no more than 120 bits, associated data A and plaintext P, and returns a ciphertext of bitlen(P) + TAGLEN bits. OCB-DECRYPT takes K, N, A and a ciphertext of at least TAGLEN bits.

Both directions work block by block. Each 128-bit block is combined with a running offset, passed through the block cipher, and combined with the offset again, while a checksum of the plaintext blocks is accumulated. A final partial block is padded and handled with a separate offset. The tag is a block-cipher output over the checksum, XORed with the hash of the associated data and cut to TAGLEN bits.

On decryption, if the computed tag does not equal the tag carried in the ciphertext, the function produces INVALID instead of a plaintext.
sections.eli5: The message is cut into pieces. Each piece is scrambled with a different twist, and a running total is kept to make the seal. If the seal does not match when opened, the box is rejected.

sections.title: Security Limits and Nonces
sections.content:
OCB aims at confidentiality (outputs look like random bits) and authenticity (an attacker cannot produce a new valid nonce and ciphertext pair). These hold only if the block cipher is a strong pseudorandom permutation, so a conservatively designed, well-trusted cipher such as AES should be used. Both properties degrade as s^2 / 2^128, where s is the total number of blocks the adversary sees. A given key should encrypt at most 2^48 blocks (2^55 bits or 4 petabytes), including associated data, and automated key management is recommended for large volumes.

The nonce is critical. Reusing a nonce with the same key and different plaintexts undermines confidentiality and all authenticity protection, and the attacker can recover secret authenticity information, which makes forgery trivial. Nonces need not be secret and may be counters. If two parties share a key, their nonce spaces must be partitioned, for example odd and even counters. OCB is not suited to environments without reliable nonces; the RFC points to SIV for those.

Other points: a forgery succeeds with probability 2^-TAGLEN, a key should normally use a single tag length, timing and power attacks are outside the formal model, and the ciphertext reveals the plaintext length.
sections.eli5: Never use the same one-time number twice with the same key, or the lock stops protecting you. And do not use one key for too much data.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added nine entries to its registry for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data parameters, one for each named parameter set in Section 3.1. Their numeric IDs run from 20 to 28, starting with AEAD_AES_128_OCB_TAGLEN128 as 20 and ending with AEAD_AES_256_OCB_TAGLEN64 as 28.

Appendix A supplies sample results for OCB with AES: sixteen (nonce, associated data, plaintext, ciphertext) tuples under a fixed key and a 128-bit tag, so implementers can check their code.
sections.eli5: Each version of OCB got an official number in a public list, so everyone calls it by the same name.
